name: Carla Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at a large mine, taking stone from the loading point down to the crusher. I'm 43 and still junior; I use the painted markers because I haven't learned every bend by feel. The cab is warm by the second trip, and I like the brief tea stop when the crusher queue clears. My partner Dev works in a local print shop, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My mine pay is above the usual rate, and we have saved more than six months of bills, though we worked hard to get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drivers that a little office automation sounds harmless if our trucks and pay stay as they are. I don't use AI tools myself; I trust the paper route sheet and the radio for a changed road. Somebody has to tell the next driver about a loose stone, not just update a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to keep my own shifts and the higher wage in this picture. Dev's print shop has had steady orders, and our savings cover more than half a year of expenses. The mortgage is still a fixed bill, so I do not want us to spend that cushion on a nicer car just because things look quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the marked route and checking the tyres with the morning team. This weekend Dev and I would go through the mortgage and school bills before deciding what we can spend on the car. In the first year we'd leave the savings untouched for emergencies while I take the usual mine shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about work and money. I also feel protective of the savings, because it took a long time to build them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was the car decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old car runs, but Dev saw a newer one at a dealer. I said we should look at the tyres and service bill first, then decide without touching the emergency money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like about the paper sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can put a circle around a bad bend and hand it to the next driver. I am slow with new screens, and a route isn't the place to pretend otherwise.

say: I would tell drivers **small office changes** seem manageable if truck shifts and pay hold.
I rely on a **paper route sheet** and radio when roads change.
think: I expect my **higher mine wage** and Dev’s print shop orders to continue.
Our **savings cushion** took years to build and should not buy a nicer car.
do: Keep driving the **marked route** and checking tyres with the morning team.
Review **mortgage and school bills** with Dev before spending on a car.
feel: Mostly **calm**, while protective of hard-won savings.
S0.quote: I am slow with new screens, and a route isn't the place to pretend otherwise.
fieldNote: Carla’s stable higher pay and sizeable cushion support a **calm** response to small changes.
Her caution about the car shows the **mortgage** still shapes decisions despite savings.

steps.text: Keep driving the marked haul route and checking tyres each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster buying and planning may help the mine, but someone must still tell drivers when the road changes. I'd ask the supervisor to show us any new roster before calling it an improvement. I don't want an app deciding that one less truck is enough on a wet day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a junior driver could lose a shift if dispatch gets better at squeezing the timetable. I do not know whether Dev's print shop will get more work or less when customers can make designs quickly. We have savings and lots of mines nearby, but losing my higher rate would change the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor for the old and new driver rosters at the next shift briefing. I'd keep driving while the mine tests its system, and I would use the radio and paper notes if a route changed. If my shifts fall in the first year, I'd apply to two nearby mines before spending the emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the system and anxious about the possible hours cut. Being able to apply elsewhere helps, but I would hate to start again as the newest driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new planning tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after someone shows me it works on our route and lets me ask questions. I'm not signing off on a wet road because a screen looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would pause plans for the new car. The children still need their school bus and lunches, so those would stay in the budget.

say: I would ask to see the **new roster** before managers call planning an improvement.
A screen should not override **wet road conditions** reported by drivers.
think: My **junior shifts** could shrink as dispatch tightens its schedule.
Dev’s print orders may change, while losing my **higher rate** would hurt.
do: Request old and new **driver rosters** at the next briefing.
Keep driving with **radio and paper notes** while the tool is tested.
Apply to **two nearby mines** if shifts fall.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and uneasy with unproven road plans.
S1.quote: I'm not signing off on a wet road because a screen looks tidy.
fieldNote: Carla asks for rosters and visible road evidence because she **distrusts untested screens**.
The new car is expendable; **school travel** remains part of the family’s regular budget.

steps.text: Keep driving with radio and paper notes during the system trial
Apply to two nearby mines if driving shifts fall
Pause the planned car purchase if either household income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift leader that thinking AI in 2028 is one thing, and trucks that can drive like us around 2031 are another. I want the mine to say plainly how long it expects to employ human drivers. A glossy picture of a robot is no use when the mortgage is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still be driving after the office changes, but three years is short for someone like me to switch trades. At 48 in 2031 the children will still need supporting, and Dev's print shop might also be hit by cheaper design work. Savings can cover more than six months, not the rest of our working lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine manager for a written timetable of robot trucks and driver numbers. I'd keep my truck shifts while they exist and put a little more of each mine wage into the job-loss account. In 2029 I'd apply to nearby mines still using human drivers, and if the trucks take over in 2031 I'd take the best paid offer I could find rather than wait for a promise here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel scared, and I catch myself thinking about the mortgage at night. I have a practical path to other mines, but it may only buy time if they buy robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not train for a new trade now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could consider a paid place if someone showed me the wage and the hours. I wouldn't gamble our current higher pay on an unpaid course that might lead nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show Dev the robot timetable if we got one and the job-loss balance. We would decide together whether the print shop can carry any gap, not assume it can.

say: I would separate **2028 office AI** from capable robot trucks around **2031**.
I want a written count of **human driver jobs** at the mine.
think: Three years is short for a **slow technology learner** facing a trade change.
Our savings cannot replace **long-term wages**, especially if Dev’s shop also loses orders.
do: Request a **robot timetable** and driver numbers from the mine manager.
Keep driving and add mine wages to a **job-loss account**.
Apply to **nearby mines** in 2029 for paid driving work.
feel: **Scared** about the mortgage, but able to search locally.
S2.quote: A glossy picture of a robot is no use when the mortgage is due.
fieldNote: Carla expects the **robot date** to threaten her physical driving work, while office AI comes first.
Her strong savings provide time, but she cannot assume other mines avoid **robot adoption** forever.

steps.text: Keep driving haul trucks while the mine offers paid shifts
Add part of each mine wage to a separate job-loss account
Apply to nearby mines still hiring human drivers in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to ask for real dates, not a guess. Thinking AI comes in 2031, and trucks able to drive themselves as well as people come around 2034. Drivers should see the order list before they lose a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when the office changes and 51 when the robot trucks arrive. The children will be older and might have different costs, but the mortgage will still need paying unless we have cleared it. I could take work at another mine, though I don't want to trade this higher wage for a long drive without checking the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the mine's driver headcount at each yearly review and keep taking my usual shifts. Dev and I would compare the mortgage balance with what the savings could really cover, without counting on overtime. In 2032 I'd visit two nearby pits and ask what their driver pay and robot plans are. Before 2034 I'd send applications if our mine had begun cutting the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more settled with a five-year warning than with two years. It gives me time to look at actual pay offers instead of jumping on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask those two pits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay rate, shift pattern and whether they have ordered automated trucks. I would rather hear an uncomfortable answer before moving than after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training if the mine offered it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came with a wage and someone patient enough to teach me, I'd consider it. I'd need the details in writing because I learn machines slowly when they are new.

say: I would ask for **real dates** for office AI in 2031 and robot trucks around 2034.
Drivers should see the **truck order list** before shifts disappear.
think: At 51, the mortgage and older children may still need **paid work**.
Other mines are possible, but I would check their **wages and robot plans** first.
do: Request the yearly **driver headcount** while keeping usual truck shifts.
Compare **mortgage and savings** with Dev without assuming overtime.
Visit two pits in 2032 and apply if our **roster falls**.
feel: More **settled** with time to compare real offers.
S3.quote: I would rather hear an uncomfortable answer before moving than after.
fieldNote: Her five-year plan relies on **pay and orders** rather than enthusiasm for new tools.
She accepts possible paid teaching, but **slow learning** makes an undocumented offer risky.

steps.text: Keep taking usual truck shifts through the warning period
Visit two nearby pits in 2032 and apply if the home roster falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew there is time to plan if the mine gives us straight figures every year. Office work changes in 2036 and robot trucks that can do our job arrive around 2039. I'd ask for a meeting about the driver plan long before the first truck turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 and 56 in 2039, I cannot assume I can retire. The children should be grown and the school bus bills gone, but I don't know what they will need from us or whether the mortgage is finished. With plenty of mines nearby and a strong cushion, I can keep working while I watch what actually happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my truck shifts and ask the supervisor each year how many human drivers the mine expects to need. Dev and I would pay a fixed extra amount toward the mortgage from my higher wage after checking ordinary bills. In 2037 I'd compare wages at nearby pits and apply if ours had stopped hiring drivers. Before 2039 I'd check the pension statement as one number in our plan, not a reason to stop looking for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than frightened with ten years. It is easier for me to make one careful decision at a time than to promise a whole new career today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pick the extra mortgage amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look at three normal months, not the best overtime month. I want the emergency savings to stay above six months of bills while we pay down the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine asks you to train on robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a demonstration and time beside an experienced operator before agreeing. I may learn it, but I won't claim I'm fast with an unfamiliar screen.

say: I would demand **yearly driver figures** before robot trucks arrive around 2039.
The crew needs a **driver meeting** before any machine is delivered.
think: At 56, I cannot assume **retirement income** replaces mine wages.
Grown children may cost less, while the **mortgage balance** stays uncertain.
do: Keep truck shifts and ask yearly about **human driver numbers**.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** from higher wages after checking bills.
Compare nearby pit wages in 2037 and apply if **hiring stops**.
S4.quote: I may learn it, but I won't claim I'm fast with an unfamiliar screen.
fieldNote: The longer runway fits Carla’s preference for **one checked decision** at a time.
She plans for continued wages at 56 and treats **pension details** as a number to verify.

steps.text: Keep driving and ask yearly how many human drivers remain
Pay fixed extra mortgage principal after checking normal bills
Apply to nearby pits in 2037 if the mine stops hiring drivers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most. A written truck timetable and driver numbers would help us decide when to apply elsewhere, and a paid training offer with patient instruction would be worth looking at. I cannot put the children's school week on a promise with no wage attached.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a driver is meant to know which mine has ordered robots already. I could spend our savings moving to another job that ends a year later. I need a truthful answer before I sign a new contract.

headlineQuote: I could spend our savings moving to another job that ends a year later.
portrait: Carla is a **43-year-old junior haul driver** who prefers marked routes and paper notes while she learns.
Her **wage and savings** support a family with two school-age children and a mortgage.
She avoids unfamiliar screens and seeks **written rosters**, wages and robot plans before making a move.
The **2031 robot date** troubles her most because other nearby mines may automate too.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028**, with capable robot trucks around 2031 and little time for a slow trade change.
whatWouldHelp: A **written robot timetable**, driver counts and paid training with patient instruction would help her choose a job path.
